chapter.title: Objects and Values
chapter.para: These recipes are about the shape of .NET values in Rexx: enums, parameters by reference, objects that must be disposed, errors, and finding out what an object can do.

section.title: Enums and Flags
section.para: You want to use .NET's enum values, flags included, in Rexx's terms.

example.title: Enums and Flags
example.programlisting:
attrs = .net~System~IO~FileAttributes a = .net~as("ReadOnly, Hidden", attrs) f = .net~System~Enum~Parse(.net~typeObject(attrs), "ReadOnly, Hidden") say f f~ordinal f~HasFlag(attrs~Hidden) (f = "hidden, readonly") d = .net~System~DateTime~new(2026, 10, 18)~DayOfWeek select when d = "Saturday" | d = "Sunday" then say d "is a weekend day" otherwise say d "is a weekday" end do with index n item name over .net~System~ConsoleColor if n < 3 then say n name end
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: ReadOnly, Hidden 3 1 1 Sunday is a weekend day 0 Black 1 DarkBlue 2 DarkGreen

section.para: How it works. An enum value is a NetEnum: its string is its name, so SAY and WHEN d = "Saturday" work as with a string, and = compares with a name (caseless; flags in any order) or a number. ordinal is its number. .NET's own methods (HasFlag) work on it. An enum type gives its numbers and names with DO WITH. Where .NET wants an enum, a name works too: form~StartPosition = "CenterScreen".
See also Reference, Classes, NetEnum Class.

section.title: out and ref Parameters
section.para: You want to call a method that returns values through its parameters, as TryParse.

example.title: out and ref Parameters
example.programlisting:
n = .net~ref do s over .array~of("42", "x", " 7 ") if .net~System~Int32~TryParse(s, n) then say "'"s"' is" n~value else say "'"s"' is no int" end d = .net~ref say .net~System~DateTime~TryParse("2026-10-16", d) d~value~Year q = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Queue<string>")~new item = .net~ref say q~TryDequeue(item) item~value
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: '42' is 42 'x' is no int ' 7 ' is 7 1 2026 0 The NIL object

section.para: How it works. A parameter by reference takes a NetRef; the call keeps its own result (1 or 0 here), and the NetRef's value holds what the method put in the parameter. One NetRef can serve many calls.
See also Reference, Arrays, Collections and References, ref, out and in Parameters.

section.title: Disposing of Objects
section.para: You want to close files, connections and the like at once, as C#'s using does.

example.title: Disposing of Objects
example.programlisting:
io = .net~System~IO file = io~Path~GetTempFileName w = io~StreamWriter~new(file) do i = 1 to 3; w~WriteLine("line" i); end w~Dispose -- flushes and closes: C#'s using r = io~StreamReader~new(file) do while \r~EndOfStream; say r~ReadLine; end r~Dispose io~File~Delete(file) say io~File~Exists(file)
::requires "net.cls"

section.para: How it works. Rexx collects a proxy when it is no longer used, and .NET collects the object later still: too late for a file that must be flushed and closed, or a connection that must go back to its pool. Call Dispose (or Close) when you are done, as C#'s using does. Signal handlers and SIGNAL ON traps are where to put it when errors may come first.
See also Reference, Values, By Reference.

section.title: Catching .NET's Exceptions
section.para: You want to handle the exceptions that .NET throws.

example.title: Catching .NET's Exceptions
example.programlisting: signal on syntax x = .net~System~IO~File~ReadAllText("/no/such/dir/file.txt") say "not reached" syntax: c = condition("O") e = c~additional[2] say .net~typeOf(e) say "message:" e~Message~left(30)"..." say "is an IOException:" .net~isInstance(e, "System.IO.IOException") ::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: System.IO.DirectoryNotFoundException message: Could not find a part of the p... is an IOException: 1

section.para: How it works. A .NET exception is SYNTAX 98.900 in Rexx, and the exception itself is condition("O")~additional[2], and its stack trace is additional[3]: its type (.net~typeOf), its Message, and whether it is of a family (.net~isInstance(e, "System.IO.IOException"), as C#'s catch (IOException)).

section.title: What Can This Object Do?
section.para: You want to find out, from Rexx, what a .NET object offers.

example.title: What Can This Object Do?
example.programlisting:
sb = .net~System~Text~StringBuilder~new say .net~typeOf(sb) m = .net~members(sb) say m~hasItem("AppendLine") m~hasItem("Length") m~hasItem("Nope") t = .net~typeObject(sb) do mi over t~GetMethods if mi~Name = "AppendLine", mi~GetParameters~items = 1 then say mi~ToString end say t~Assembly~GetName~Name t~BaseType~FullName say .net~isInstance(sb, "System.Runtime.Serialization.ISerializable")
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: System.Text.StringBuilder 1 1 0 System.Text.StringBuilder AppendLine(System.String) System.Text.StringBuilder AppendLine(AppendInterpolatedStringHandler ByRef) System.Private.CoreLib System.Object 1

section.para: How it works. .net~typeOf(o) names its type, .net~members(o) lists its public members, and .net~typeObject(o) is its System.Type, the way into .NET's reflection: methods with their signatures, its assembly, its base type. The type's page in .NET's documentation (https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/) says the rest.
See also Reference, Classes, NetGlobal Class (the .net Object).
